content: The findings of this review were instrumental in shaping the design of the World Health Organization (WHO) Guidance for After Action Reviews (AARs) and the associated comprehensive toolkits. These resources aim to assist Member States in planning, preparing, and conducting AARs to facilitate collective learning and operational improvements following public health responses. This paper is specifically directed at professionals in health, humanitarian, and development sectors, as well as organizations involved in the applied use of knowledge management techniques for monitoring, evaluating performance, country planning, and operations within the context of health emergency preparedness and response. The review begins with a detailed explanation of the methodology used for the literature search, followed by the presentation of findings. The results encompass a wide range of topics, including the foundational principles and origins of AAR theories, their benefits and objectives, evaluation systems, knowledge management theories and methodologies, lessons learned, and implications derived from real-world applications of AARs since their inception by the United States Army in the 1970s. The screening methodology for the literature involved selecting sources based on their titles, abstracts, and keywords. The search was conducted in multiple interconnected stages, starting with a high-level search using interdisciplinary databases such as PubMed, MEDLINE, and SAGE Journals Online, among others. Additional sources were identified through references in previously consulted documents. There were no restrictions on country or study type to ensure a comprehensive range of contexts was included. Experts from various institutions were also consulted to identify additional references. The search strategy combined free text, acronyms, and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) to optimize the capture of relevant literature within the available time. The inclusion criteria required sources to be related to at least one of the review questions, produced between 1982 and 2017, written in English, French, Italian, or Spanish, and with full text available. Sources unrelated to the review questions were excluded. A literature review matrix was created in Microsoft Excel to organize sources, key information, and metadata, with tables and boxes in the document derived from this matrix. The review identified 122 documents, of which 66 were classified as methodological (technical guidelines on AARs or other knowledge management techniques) and 56 as reports of AARs or other post-event reviews. Of the 66 methodological pieces, two were deemed non-relevant, and five were fairly relevant. Of the 56 reports, 12 were considered non-relevant. Ultimately, 107 relevant documents were included in the review. AARs are defined as knowledge-sharing and learning-focused tools conducted at the conclusion of an emergency response. They bring together teams to openly and honestly discuss successes and failures, with the goal of learning from the experience and applying lessons learned to improve future performance. AARs provide team members with the opportunity to analyze their behavior, its impact on outcomes, and potential changes needed. There is no standardized definition of AARs across sectors and disciplines. Initially derived from military practices, AARs were recognized as professional discussions focused on performance standards. However, further research has shown that AARs can be applied more broadly to review various issues using diverse data collection, facilitation, and analysis methods. AARs are both a specific knowledge management evaluation tool with a defined methodology and an approach for capturing lessons that can benefit from various methodologies and depths of review. AARs contribute to a culture of continuous learning, are relatively quick and inexpensive to conduct, and rely on open, honest, and equal interaction among participants. They follow a consistent analytical structure based on four main research questions: what should have happened, what actually happened, what went well and what did not, and what can be improved and how. AARs are systematic yet qualitative tools for reviewing planned actions, identifying strengths, weaknesses, and lessons to enhance organizational learning and response capacity. They are applicable to almost any event and can provide valuable insights even when conducted after successful experiences. AARs are effective for continuous assessment of organizational performance, capturing key learning during critical junctures, and generating recommendations for improving emergency policies and practices. AARs also help identify root causes of successes and failures, develop strategies to mitigate causal factors, and track progress to ensure planned outcomes are achieved. The primary benefits of AARs arise from applying their results to future situations, enabling teams to improve and perform to higher standards. By the end of an AAR, participants should clearly understand what worked well, what did not, and where improvements can be made. When conducted in an environment of openness, honest discussion, and commitment to identifying solutions, AARs can prevent oversimplified interpretations of response narratives, enhance operational sensitivity and resilience, and acknowledge individual expertise. They provide a structured analytical framework for identifying lessons and best practices, focusing on learning and performance as primary objectives. AARs are particularly relevant for healthcare, humanitarian, and emergency professionals who operate under constant time pressure. They help identify successful elements of a response and areas for improvement, capturing valuable knowledge and learning. The feedback generated compares actual outputs with projected outcomes, identifies organizational strengths and weaknesses, and fosters shared learning experiences that improve task proficiency and relationships among team members. Additional benefits include documenting lessons learned, advocating for financial or technical support, promoting ownership through consensus on follow-up activities, and systematizing and sharing information among peers or stakeholders facing similar challenges. Results can be recorded in registries for future reference during crises. Key features of effective AARs include leadership engagement, equal participation, stakeholder inclusion, a positive feedback environment, and the generation of shared knowledge. Observational learning, understanding individual and group perceptions, and goal setting are critical components of the AAR process. Feedback is central to AARs, providing individuals with information on areas for future improvement. Team dynamics are also essential, as participants are interdependent and function as a cohesive unit. AARs are structured around four main questions: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why was there a difference, and what can we learn from this? This model, originally developed by the U.S. Army in the 1970s, has been adapted for use in emergencies by international companies, fire brigades, and the healthcare sector.
